Summary: Moody’s kept the US sovereign rating at Aa1 with a stable outlook after its regular review The agency said the economy has outperformed its expectations, with Q3 real GDP growth of 3.4% annualised Growth is forecast at 2.3% this year, then around 2% in both 2027 and 2028 AI infrastructure spending is supporting near-term growth and may lift productivity, though the scale of the gains is uncertain Higher interest rates, elevated energy prices and a normalising AI investment cycle are seen as drags on growth Moody’s cited innovation, a dynamic private sector, deep capital markets, the dollar’s reserve status and an independent Fed as key strengths Moody’s Ratings said the US economy has performed better than it initially expected in 2026, and it kept the country’s Aa1 sovereign rating with a stable outlook in its regular review of US creditworthiness. The agency pointed to real GDP growth of 3.4% at an annualised pace in the third quarter and now expects growth of 2.3% for the full year, before a slowdown to around 2% in both 2027 and 2028. Artificial intelligence features on both sides of that outlook. Moody’s said heavy spending on AI infrastructure is propping up growth in the near term and could eventually deliver lasting productivity gains, although it stressed that the size of those gains is still uncertain. At the same time, it expects the AI investment cycle to normalise, which would remove some of the support that has driven this year’s outperformance. The agency listed two other headwinds alongside that: higher interest rates and energy prices that remain elevated. Both are live issues. Several Federal Reserve officials have argued this week for further tightening, and oil markets remain on edge over shipping risks in the Middle East. Against those pressures, Moody’s said the economy’s capacity for innovation, a dynamic private sector and deep capital markets should continue to support investment and productivity over time. The rating rationale leans heavily on institutional strengths. Moody’s cited the country’s very high creditworthiness, its resilience to shocks and the dollar’s role as the world’s reserve currency. It also said it expects the US to maintain its long record of effective monetary policy led by an independent Federal Reserve. That point is more than a formality: Fed independence is one of the pillars the rating rests on, so any perceived erosion of it would sit squarely within what the agency is watching. For investors, the review offers reassurance without much drama. A stable outlook signals that Moody’s sees no near-term pressure for a change in either direction, and its growth forecasts broadly match the picture of an economy that is running hotter than expected but set to cool as rates bite and the AI spending surge matures. The bigger question for markets is whether that late-year strength keeps the Fed on its hiking path into December. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

Today Waller renewed his call for 50 basis points. “October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” said NAR Chief Economist Dr. Lawrence Yun. “Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s,” Yun added. “It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.” For background, the National Association of Realtors publishes its Pending Home Sales Index monthly at 10 am ET, usually near the end of the month. It tracks signed contracts to buy existing homes, including single-family homes, condos and co-ops, making it the most forward-looking piece of NAR’s monthly housing data. The index is benchmarked so that 100 equals the average level of contract activity in 2001, a year NAR considers a normal, balanced market. Readings are seasonally adjusted and reported as monthly and year-over-year changes. Results are also broken down by region: Northeast, Midwest, South and West. Because a home sale typically closes one to two months after a contract is signed, pending sales lead NAR’s existing home sales report, which counts completed closings. Economists use the index to gauge where existing home sales are headed. The relationship isn’t perfect. Some contracts fall through because of financing problems, failed inspections or appraisal gaps, and cancellation rates can rise when mortgage rates jump or buyers get cold feet. Contract signings are highly sensitive to mortgage rates, so the index often responds quickly to moves in Treasury yields. A drop in rates can show up in pending sales within weeks, well before it appears in closings or prices. The report rarely moves broader markets, but it’s watched closely by homebuilder and mortgage-related stocks and as an early read on housing demand. In recent years, the index has hovered near historically low levels as high mortgage rates, stretched affordability and the lock-in effect, where homeowners are reluctant to give up low-rate mortgages, have kept buyers and sellers on the sidelines. The one positive was unemployment, which edged down to 5.1% from 5.2%. Even so, economists do not expect a rush of new policy. With third-quarter growth at 4.5%, Beijing still looks on track for its annual target, and some analysts said they expect no new stimulus for the rest of the year. Others described 2026 as one of the weakest years for domestic demand in recent history. They said support for consumption could build in 2027, especially if exports start to cool and the drag from earlier trade-in subsidies fades. For now, the AI export boom is carrying growth, and analysts say Beijing is likely to step up support for domestic demand only if that tailwind starts to fade. title: TSMC reportedly demands cash up front from AI chip clients amid circular financing fears
summary: If confirmed, the move would be a vote of caution about AI customer finances from the company with the clearest view of chip demand. That would add weight to the circular financing debate that has hung over AI stocks this month. Custom chip designers and smaller AI players with stretched balance sheets would face tighter cash flow and could lose capacity to better-funded rivals. For TSMC, the policy would strengthen its pricing power and reduce its credit risk, a positive for the stock and for Taiwan’s tech-heavy market. Watch for any confirmation or denial from TSMC, which would set how seriously the report is taken. --- While Nvidia extends credit to the AI boom, TSMC is reportedly asking its customers to show the money first, and that difference says a lot about who carries the risk. Summary: TSMC is reportedly setting credit limits for customers based on their balance sheets, payment history and default risk Orders above the limit must reportedly be paid in cash, and some customers must prepay to secure capacity The policy mainly affects custom AI chip makers, several of which are raising money through bonds, equity and loans The report links the change to concerns about circular financing in AI TSMC has not announced the policy, and the outlet could not confirm it independently TSMC has begun weighing customers’ finances before handing out chipmaking capacity, setting credit limits and asking some buyers to pay cash up front, Chinese technology outlet Kuai Keji reported, citing industry sources. TSMC has not announced the policy, and the outlet said it could not independently confirm it. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, or TSMC, is the world’s largest contract chipmaker. It does not design its own chips. Instead, it manufactures them for companies such as Nvidia, Apple, AMD and the growing number of firms building custom AI processors. Founded in Hsinchu in 1987, it produces the vast majority of the world’s most advanced chips. That gives it near-monopoly control of the capacity every AI company needs, and that leverage is what lets it set terms on who gets served first. According to the report, TSMC now sets a credit limit for each customer based on its balance sheet. The assessment reportedly covers any history of late or unpaid bills, the customer’s standing in the industry, its business outlook and the estimated loss if it defaulted. Orders above that limit must be paid in cash, and some customers must prepay to secure their allocated capacity. The change is said to apply mainly to makers of custom AI chips, several of which are raising money through overseas convertible bonds, equity sales and syndicated bank loans. The report links the shift directly to concerns about circular financing in the AI industry, where companies invest in one another and then buy from each other. In effect, TSMC would be moving from allocating capacity on a first-come, first-served basis to asking customers to prove they can pay. That fits with comments from chief executive C.C. Wei, who has said on an earnings call that capacity planning takes into account cloud providers’ capital spending, their financial condition, and the availability of power and components. TSMC has also sent staff to the United States to check on data centre construction. The company already holds large customer prepayments, around NT$234 billion at the end of June, although Kuai Keji noted these are standard accounting prepayments rather than the new credit system. The contrast with Nvidia is striking. Nvidia is increasingly acting as a financier of the AI build-out, with commitments of about $518 billion and customer receivables of about $81 billion, according to its latest results and a Financial Times report. TSMC, sitting further up the supply chain with near-monopoly control of advanced chipmaking, appears to be heading the other way, shifting risk back onto its customers. If confirmed, the policy would tighten cash flow for chip designers that already tie up large sums in design and packaging costs, and it would favour well-funded customers over smaller players. It would also be a sign that the company best placed to judge AI demand wants protection in case some of its customers cannot pay. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
